title: Parts of Speech
subtitle: The 9 word classes

content.introduction: An adjective is a word that describes or gives information about a noun or pronoun.
content.urduExplanation: اسم صفت وہ لفظ ہے جو کسی اسم یا اسم ضمیر کی خصوصیت، مقدار، تعداد، ملکیت یا نشاندہی کے بارے میں معلومات دے۔
content.englishExplanation: Adjectives modify nouns and pronouns, answering questions like which one, what kind, or how many. They typically appear before the noun they describe or after a linking verb as a subject complement. Adjectives have three degrees of comparison: positive (tall), comparative (taller), and superlative (tallest), used to compare two or more things. Some adjectives are descriptive (happy, red), while others indicate quantity (few, many), possession (my, her), or demonstration (this, those). Correct comparative and superlative forms, along with proper word order, are essential for accurate English.

types.name: Adjective of Quality
types.description: Adjective of Quality tells us about the quality or kind of a person or thing.
types.urduExplanation: Adjective of quality ہمیں کسی شخص یا چیز کی خاصیت یا قسم کے بارے میں بتاتا ہے۔
types.exampleWords: honest, brave, beautiful, intelligent, difficult
rules: Ask **"What kind?"** to identify it.
It can describe a person, place, animal, or thing.
It can come before a noun.
It can come after a linking verb.
ruleExamples: He is **an honest** man. > What kind of man? **Honest**

Person: She is **intelligent**.
Place: It is a **peaceful** city.
Animal: The dog is **loyal**.
Thing: He bought an **expensive** car.

She is a **beautiful** girl.
He bought an **expensive** phone.

The girl is **beautiful**.
The food smells **delicious**.
The child became **angry**.

examples.text: Ali is a **brave** soldier.
examples.urdu: علی ایک بہادر سپاہی ہے۔
examples.note: **Brave** describes the quality of the soldier.

examples.text: She lives in a **beautiful** house.
examples.urdu: وہ ایک خوبصورت گھر میں رہتی ہے۔
examples.note: **Beautiful** describes the quality of the house.

examples.text: The **difficult** question confused the students.
examples.urdu: مشکل سوال نے طلبہ کو الجھن میں ڈال دیا۔
examples.note: **Difficult** describes the question.

examples.text: The loyal dog guarded the peaceful home.
examples.urdu: وفادار کتے نے پُرامن گھر کی حفاظت کی۔
examples.note: **Loyal** and **peaceful** describe qualities.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہ ایک ایماندار آدمی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: A singular countable noun needs the article **an** before the adjective and noun.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہ ایک خوبصورت لڑکی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: **Beautiful** is the adjective used to describe the girl; **beauty** is a noun.

commonMistakes.urdu: کھانا مزیدار خوشبو دے رہا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: After the linking verb **smells**, use the adjective **delicious**, not the adverb **deliciously**.

commonMistakes.urdu: اس نے ایک مہنگا فون خریدا۔
commonMistakes.note: The adjective must describe a noun; **expensive** needs a noun such as phone.

types.name: Adjective of Quantity
types.description: An Adjective of Quantity tells us how much of a thing is meant.
types.urduExplanation: صفت مقدار وہ لفظ ہے جو کسی اسم کی مقدار کو ظاہر کرے، یعنی یہ بتائے کہ کسی چیز کی کتنی مقدار ہے۔
types.exampleWords: much, little, some, enough, sufficient, no
rules: It tells the amount of something.
It is mainly used with **uncountable nouns**.
Do not confuse quantity with number.
**little** and **a little** have different meanings.
Some words can be used with both countable and uncountable nouns, but their meaning changes.
ruleExamples:
I have **some** money.
There is **little** water. > An adjective of quantity answers **"How much?"**

**much water**
**little milk**
**enough food**

**much water** > Quantity > How much
**many books** > Number > How many
**Uncountable noun** > Quantity
**Countable noun** > Number

He has **little** money. > Almost no money.
He has **a little** money. > Some money.
**little** = almost none
**a little** = some

**some water** > amount of water.
**some books** > number of books. > Always look at the noun and ask whether the word indicates amount or number.

examples.text: There is **little** water in the bottle.
examples.urdu: بوتل میں تھوڑا پانی ہے۔
examples.note: **Little** shows a small amount of uncountable water.

examples.text: She has **enough** knowledge for the examination.
examples.urdu: اس کے پاس امتحان کے لیے کافی علم ہے۔
examples.note: **Enough** shows a sufficient amount of knowledge.

examples.text: He has **a little** money for the journey.
examples.urdu: اس کے پاس سفر کے لیے کچھ رقم ہے۔
examples.note: **A little** means some amount, though not much.

examples.text: There is **some** water in the glass, and there are **some** books on the desk.
examples.urdu: گلاس میں کچھ پانی ہے اور میز پر کچھ کتابیں ہیں۔
examples.note: **Some** can show an amount with water and a number with books.

commonMistakes.urdu: میرے پاس زیادہ پانی نہیں ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Water is uncountable, so use **much** for its amount.

commonMistakes.wrong: There are **much books** on the table.
commonMistakes.right: There are **many books** on the table.
commonMistakes.urdu: میز پر بہت سی کتابیں ہیں۔
commonMistakes.note: Books are countable and plural, so use **many** for their number.

commonMistakes.wrong: He has **little money**, so he can buy everything.
commonMistakes.right: He has **a little money**, so he can buy something.
commonMistakes.urdu: اس کے پاس کچھ رقم ہے، اس لیے وہ کچھ خرید سکتا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: **Little** means almost none, while **a little** means some.

commonMistakes.urdu: مجھے کچھ پانی چاہیے۔
commonMistakes.note: Water is normally uncountable, so do not use **a** directly before it.

types.name: Adjective of Number
types.description: An adjective of number is a word that tells us how many persons or things are meant or in what order they occur.
types.urduExplanation: صفتِ عدد وہ لفظ ہے جو کسی اسم کی تعداد یا ترتیب کو ظاہر کرے۔
types.exampleWords: one, two, many, few, several, first, second
rules: It tells us how many persons or things there are.
It is generally used with countable nouns.
**Few** and **a few** have different meanings.
ruleExamples:
Five students passed the test.
Several candidates applied for the job. > An adjective of number answers **"How many?"**

Three books
Many students
Two cars > Adjectives of number generally describe countable nouns.

Few students passed the test. > Almost none.
A few students passed the test. > Some students.
**Few** = almost none
**A few** = some

examples.text: Five students passed the test.
examples.urdu: پانچ طلبہ امتحان میں کامیاب ہوئے۔
examples.note: **Five** tells us how many students passed.

examples.text: Several candidates applied for the job.
examples.urdu: کئی امیدواروں نے ملازمت کے لیے درخواست دی۔
examples.note: **Several** shows an indefinite number of countable candidates.

examples.text: The first candidate answered the question.
examples.urdu: پہلے امیدوار نے سوال کا جواب دیا۔
examples.note: **First** shows the order of the candidate.

examples.text: A few students attended the seminar.
examples.urdu: چند طلبہ نے سیمینار میں شرکت کی۔
examples.note: **A few** means some students, not almost none.

commonMistakes.urdu: بہت سے طلبہ امتحان میں کامیاب ہوئے۔
commonMistakes.note: Students are countable and plural, so use **many** for number, not **much** for quantity.

commonMistakes.urdu: تین طلبہ امتحان میں کامیاب ہوئے۔
commonMistakes.note: A number greater than one normally takes a plural countable noun.

commonMistakes.wrong: ❌ Few students passed, so the hall was full.
commonMistakes.right: ✅ A few students passed, so the hall was not empty.
commonMistakes.urdu: چند طلبہ کامیاب ہوئے، اس لیے ہال خالی نہیں تھا۔
commonMistakes.note: **Few** means almost none, while **a few** means some.

commonMistakes.right: ✅ The first student entered the room.
commonMistakes.urdu: پہلا طالب علم کمرے میں داخل ہوا۔
commonMistakes.note: A singular ordinal noun usually needs a determiner such as **the** before it.

types.name: Demonstrative Adjective
types.description: A demonstrative adjective is a word used before a noun to point out a specific person, place, animal, or thing.
types.urduExplanation: صفتِ اشارہ وہ لفظ ہے جو کسی مخصوص شخص، جگہ، جانور یا چیز کی طرف اشارہ کرے اور عموماً اسم سے پہلے آئے۔
types.exampleWords: This, That, Those, These
rules: A demonstrative adjective must come before a noun.
Do not confuse demonstrative adjectives with demonstrative pronouns.
ruleExamples:
This book is useful.
Those students are hardworking. > **This**, **those** + noun = demonstrative adjective.

This book is interesting. > **This** = adjective
This is interesting. > **This** = pronoun
If the demonstrative is followed by a noun, it is a demonstrative adjective; if it stands alone, it is a demonstrative pronoun.

examples.text: This book is useful.
examples.urdu: یہ کتاب مفید ہے۔
examples.note: **This** comes before the noun book, so it is a demonstrative adjective.

examples.text: Those students are hardworking.
examples.urdu: وہ طلبہ محنتی ہیں۔
examples.note: **Those** comes before the noun students, so it points out specific students.

examples.text: These questions are important for the examination.
examples.urdu: یہ سوالات امتحان کے لیے اہم ہیں۔
examples.note: **These** points out specific questions and comes before the noun questions.

examples.text: That building is the examination hall.
examples.urdu: وہ عمارت امتحانی ہال ہے۔
examples.note: **That** points out one specific building.

commonMistakes.urdu: یہ ایک مفید کتاب ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: A singular countable noun needs an article. **This** is a demonstrative adjective, and book needs **a**.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہ میری کتابیں ہیں۔
commonMistakes.note: **Those** refers to plural books, so use the plural verb **are**, not **is**.

commonMistakes.urdu: یہ کتاب مہنگی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: A singular noun takes **this**, while a plural noun takes **these**.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہ طلبہ تیار ہیں۔
commonMistakes.note: Students is plural, so use the plural demonstrative **those**.

types.name: Possessive Adjective
types.description: A Possessive Adjective is a word that shows ownership, possession, or relationship and is used before a noun.
types.exampleWords: my, your, his, her, its, our, their

examples.text: My book is new.
examples.urdu: میری کتاب نئی ہے.
examples.note: **My** shows whose book is being discussed.

examples.text: Her brother is a doctor.
examples.urdu: اس کا بھائی ڈاکٹر ہے۔
examples.note: **Her** shows the relationship with the brother.

examples.text: His car is expensive.
examples.urdu: اس کی گاڑی مہنگی ہے۔
examples.note: **His** comes before the noun car.

examples.text: This is my book. > **My** = Possessive Adjective
examples.urdu: یہ میری کتاب ہے۔ > **My** = صفتِ ملکی
examples.note: **My** comes before book.

commonMistakes.urdu: میری کتاب نئی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Do not normally use **a, an, or the** directly before a possessive adjective.

commonMistakes.urdu: اس کی گاڑی مہنگی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Possessive adjectives do not take an apostrophe.

commonMistakes.urdu: بلی نے اپنا پنجہ صاف کیا۔
commonMistakes.note: **Its** shows possession; **it’s** means it is or it has.

commonMistakes.wrong: This book is mine. > **Mine** = Possessive Adjective
commonMistakes.right: This book is mine. > **Mine** = Possessive Pronoun
commonMistakes.urdu: یہ کتاب میری ہے۔ > **Mine** = اسمِ ضمیرِ ملکی
commonMistakes.note: **Mine** stands alone, so it is a possessive pronoun.

types.urduExplanation: صفت ملکی وہ لفظ ہے جو کسی شخص یا چیز کے ساتھ ملکیت، تعلق یا وابستگی ظاہر کرے اور عموماً اسم سے پہلے آئے۔
rules: A Possessive Adjective shows ownership, possession, or relationship.
A Possessive Adjective comes before a noun.
Do not use an article before a possessive adjective.
Do not use an apostrophe (') with possessive adjectives.
Be careful with **its** and **it's**.
Do not confuse possessive adjectives with possessive pronouns.
ruleExamples:
**My** book is new.
**Her** brother is a doctor.
Rule: It tells us **whose** person or thing is being discussed.

**His** car is expensive.
**Their** house is large.
Rule: Possessive Adjective + noun.

Incorrect: The my book
Correct: my book
Rule: Do not normally use **a, an, or the** directly before a possessive adjective.

Incorrect: Her's car.
Correct: Her car.
Rule: **my, your, his, her, its, our, their** do not take an apostrophe.

The cat cleaned it's paw. > Possession
It's raining. > It is
Rule: **Its** = Possession; **It's** = It is / It has.

This is my book. > **My** = Possessive Adjective
This book is mine. > **Mine** = Possessive Pronoun
Rule: Possessive Adjective + noun; possessive pronoun stands alone.

types.name: Interrogative Adjective
types.description: An interrogative adjective is used with a noun to ask a question.
types.urduExplanation: صفتِ استفہام اسم کے ساتھ مل کر سوال پوچھنے کے لیے استعمال ہوتی ہے۔
types.exampleWords: what, which, whose
rules: An interrogative adjective is used with a noun to ask a question.
**Whose** asks about possession or ownership.
Do not confuse an interrogative adjective with an interrogative pronoun.
Exam Shortcut: Question word + noun = Interrogative Adjective. Question word without a noun = Interrogative Pronoun.
ruleExamples:
**Which book** do you want?
**What subject** do you study? > **What**, **which**, and **whose** are common interrogative adjectives when they come before a noun.

**Whose pen** is this?
**Whose car** is parked outside? > **Whose + noun** asks who owns something.

**Which book** is yours? > **Which** = interrogative adjective because it modifies book.
**Which** is yours? > **Which** = interrogative pronoun because it stands alone.

Question word + noun > Interrogative Adjective
Question word without a noun > Interrogative Pronoun

examples.text: Which book do you want?
examples.urdu: آپ کون سی کتاب چاہتے ہیں؟
examples.note: **Which** comes before the noun book, so it is an interrogative adjective.

examples.text: What subject do you study?
examples.urdu: آپ کون سا مضمون پڑھتے ہیں؟
examples.note: **What** comes before the noun subject and asks about it.

examples.text: Whose pen is this?
examples.urdu: یہ قلم کس کا ہے؟
examples.note: **Whose** comes before pen and asks about ownership.

examples.text: Which book is yours?
examples.urdu: آپ کی کتاب کون سی ہے؟
examples.note: **Which** modifies book, so it is an interrogative adjective.

commonMistakes.urdu: آپ کون سی کتاب چاہتے ہیں؟
commonMistakes.note: The interrogative adjective must come before the noun: **which book**.

commonMistakes.urdu: یہ قلم کس کا ہے؟
commonMistakes.note: When **whose** comes before a noun, it is an interrogative adjective.

commonMistakes.urdu: آپ کون سا مضمون پڑھتے ہیں؟
commonMistakes.note: The question word comes before the noun subject, followed by the helping verb and subject.

commonMistakes.urdu: آپ کی کتاب کون سی ہے؟
commonMistakes.note: **Which** must directly come before the noun it modifies.

types.name: Distributive Adjective
types.description: Distributive Adjective refers to each person or thing in a group individually.
types.exampleWords: each, every, either, neither

examples.text: Each student has an identity card.
examples.urdu: ہر طالب علم کے پاس شناختی کارڈ ہے۔
examples.note: **Each** refers to students one by one and takes a singular verb.

examples.text: Each player received a medal.
examples.urdu: ہر کھلاڑی نے تمغہ حاصل کیا۔
examples.note: **Each** refers to every player individually.

examples.text: Every candidate needs an admit card.
examples.urdu: ہر امیدوار کو داخلہ کارڈ کی ضرورت ہے۔
examples.note: **Every** refers to all candidates individually.

examples.text: Each of the students has a book.
examples.urdu: طلبہ میں سے ہر ایک کے پاس ایک کتاب ہے۔
examples.note: **Each of** is followed by a plural noun, but the verb is singular.

commonMistakes.wrong: Each student have an identity card.
commonMistakes.right: Each student has an identity card.
commonMistakes.urdu: ہر طالب علم کے پاس شناختی کارڈ ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: **Each + singular noun** takes a singular verb.

commonMistakes.urdu: ہر طالب علم تیار ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: **Every + singular noun** takes **is**, not **are**.

commonMistakes.urdu: ہر طالب علم کو حاضر ہونا چاہیے۔
commonMistakes.note: Distributive adjectives normally take a singular countable noun.

commonMistakes.urdu: ہر کتاب مفید ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Use a singular noun after **each**.

types.urduExplanation: صفت تقسیمی وہ لفظ ہے جو کسی گروہ کے افراد یا چیزوں کو ایک ایک کرکے ظاہر کرے۔
rules: **Each** is used for individual members in a group.
**Every** refers to all members individually.
Use **of + plural noun/pronoun** after **each, either, and neither**.
Distributive Adjectives normally take a singular noun.
Do not confuse **each** and **all**.
ruleExamples:
**Each** student has an identity card.
**Each** player received a medal.
Rule: Each + singular countable noun + singular verb.

**Every** student must attend the class.
**Every** candidate needs an admit card.
Rule: Every + singular countable noun + singular verb.

**Each of** the students has a book.
**Either of** the answers is acceptable.
**Neither of** the candidates was selected.
Rule: Each/Either/Neither + of + plural noun/pronoun.

Incorrect: Every students
Correct: Every student
Incorrect: Each books
Correct: Each book
Rule: Each/Every/Either/Neither + singular countable noun.

**Each** student received a certificate. > one by one
**All** of the students received certificates. > group as a whole
Rule: Each = Individually; All = Collectively.

types.name: Proper Adjective
types.description: A proper adjective is an adjective derived from a proper noun and used to describe a person, place, culture, country, or thing.
types.urduExplanation: صفتِ خاص وہ صفت ہے جو کسی اسمِ خاص سے بنائی جائے اور کسی مخصوص شخص، جگہ، قوم، ملک یا ثقافت سے تعلق ظاہر کرے۔
types.exampleWords: Pakistani, Chinese, American
rules: A proper adjective is derived from a proper noun.
Proper adjectives can show nationality or origin.
Do not confuse a proper noun with a proper adjective.
ruleExamples:
Pakistan > Pakistani
China > Chinese > If an adjective is formed from a specific name, it is a proper adjective.

Pakistani people
Japanese technology
American history > Proper adjectives can indicate where a person, thing, or idea comes from.

Pakistan is a country. > **Pakistan** = Proper Noun
Pakistani culture is diverse. > **Pakistani** = Proper Adjective

examples.text: Pakistani people are known for their hospitality.
examples.urdu: پاکستانی لوگ اپنی مہمان نوازی کے لیے مشہور ہیں۔
examples.note: **Pakistani** is derived from Pakistan and describes people.

examples.text: We study American history.
examples.urdu: ہم امریکی تاریخ پڑھتے ہیں۔
examples.note: **American** is derived from America.

examples.text: She enjoys Chinese food.
examples.urdu: وہ چینی کھانا پسند کرتی ہے۔
examples.note: **Chinese** describes food connected with China.

examples.text: Shakespearean drama is studied in literature classes.
examples.urdu: ادب کی کلاسوں میں شیکسپیئر کے ڈرامے کا مطالعہ کیا جاتا ہے۔
examples.note: **Shakespearean** is derived from Shakespeare.

commonMistakes.urdu: پاکستانی ثقافت متنوع ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Use the proper adjective **Pakistani** to describe the noun culture.

commonMistakes.urdu: مجھے پاکستانی تاریخ پسند ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: A proper adjective does not take an apostrophe.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہ امریکی ادب پڑھتی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Use the adjective **American**, not the proper noun America, before literature.

commonMistakes.urdu: اس نے ایک چینی فون خریدا۔
commonMistakes.note: Proper adjectives derived from countries or cultures begin with a capital letter.

rules: Most one-syllable adjectives form the comparative with -er and superlative with -est (tall, taller, tallest).
Adjectives with two or more syllables usually use 'more' and 'most' instead of -er/-est (beautiful, more beautiful, most beautiful).
Never use both -er/-est and more/most together (avoid 'more taller' or 'most fastest').
Adjectives usually come before the noun they modify, but can follow linking verbs like be, seem, or become.
When multiple adjectives describe one noun, they generally follow the order: opinion, size, age, shape, color, origin, material (a beautiful small old round brown wooden table).
Some adjectives are irregular in comparison and must be memorized, such as good/better/best and bad/worse/worst.

examples.text: **Brave** Soldier, **Three** books, **Some** water, **This** pen

commonMistakes.wrong: This is more better than that one.
commonMistakes.right: This is better than that one.
commonMistakes.note: 'better' is already comparative and should not be combined with 'more'

commonMistakes.wrong: She is the most intelligentest student in class.
commonMistakes.right: She is the most intelligent student in class.
commonMistakes.note: long adjectives use only 'most', not the -est ending as well

commonMistakes.wrong: He bought a wooden beautiful old table.
commonMistakes.right: He bought a beautiful old wooden table.
commonMistakes.note: adjective order should follow opinion, age, then material

commonMistakes.wrong: This exercise is more easy than the last one.
commonMistakes.right: This exercise is easier than the last one.
commonMistakes.note: one-syllable adjectives like 'easy' typically take -er, not 'more'

practice.question: Choose the correct comparative form: 'Islamabad is ___ than Lahore in terms of planning.'
practice.explanation: 'Clean' is a short adjective, so it forms the comparative by adding -er: cleaner.

practice.question: Which sentence uses adjective order correctly?
options: She has a red small bag.
She has a small red bag.
She has a bag small red.
She has a red bag small.
practice.explanation: The correct order places size before color: small red bag.

practice.question: Select the correct superlative form of 'good'.
practice.explanation: 'Good' is irregular, and its superlative form is 'best', not a regular -est or 'most' form.

quiz.question: Choose the sentence with the correct adjective form.
options: This is the most beautifulest garden I have seen.
This is the beautifulest garden I have seen.
This is the most beautiful garden I have seen.
This is more beautiful garden I have seen.
quiz.explanation: Long adjectives like 'beautiful' use 'most' alone for the superlative, without an -est ending.

quiz.question: Which word is a possessive adjective in the sentence: 'Her essay won the competition'?
quiz.explanation: 'Her' shows ownership of the essay and modifies the noun directly, making it a possessive adjective.

quiz.question: Choose the correctly ordered sentence.
options: He bought an old round wooden table.
He bought a wooden old round table.
He bought a round old wooden table.
He bought an old wooden round table.
quiz.explanation: Correct order is age before shape before material: old round wooden table.

content.summary: Adjectives describe or modify nouns and pronouns, showing quality, quantity, or possession, and change form to express comparison. Short adjectives use -er/-est while longer ones use more/most, and irregular forms like good/better/best must be memorized. Correct adjective order and comparison forms are frequently tested and easy to master with practice.

degreeTypes.name: Positive Degree
degreeTypes.description: The Positive Degree is the basic form of an adjective. It describes the quality of a person, thing, or place without comparing it with another.
degreeTypes.urduExplanation: مثبت درجہ صفت کی بنیادی صورت ہے۔ جس میں کسی شخص، چیز یا جگہ کی خوبی یا خصوصیات بیان کی جاتی ہیں، لیکن اس کا کسی دوسرے سے موازنہ نہیں کیا جاتا۔
rules: Use the basic form of the adjective.
It normally does not make a direct comparison.
Use "as + adjective + as" to show equality.
ruleExamples:
Ali is **tall**.
She is **intelligent**.

The boy is **clever**.
The flower is **beautiful**.

Ali is **as tall as** Ahmed.
Sara is **as intelligent as** Ayesha.

examples.text: Ali is **tall**.
examples.urdu: علی لمبا ہے۔
examples.note: **Tall** is the basic form of the adjective. It describes Ali without comparing him with another person.

examples.text: The flower is **beautiful**.
examples.urdu: پھول خوبصورت ہے۔
examples.note: **Beautiful** describes the quality of one flower, so no comparative or superlative form is needed.

examples.text: Sara is **as intelligent as** Ayesha.
examples.urdu: سارہ عائشہ جتنی ذہین ہے۔
examples.note: **As intelligent as** shows that Sara and Ayesha have an equal degree of intelligence.

commonMistakes.urdu: علی لمبا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: No person or thing is being compared, so use the basic Positive form **tall**, not **taller**.

commonMistakes.urdu: لڑکا ہوشیار ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: The sentence describes one boy only. Without a comparison, use the Positive form.

commonMistakes.urdu: علی احمد جتنا لمبا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Equality uses the fixed structure **as + adjective + as**, not **as + adjective + than**.

commonMistakes.urdu: سارہ عائشہ جتنی ذہین ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Both **as** words are required to show equal quality.

commonMistakes.urdu: پھول خوبصورت ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: The sentence gives a description without a comparison, so the basic adjective form is appropriate.

degreeTypes.name: Comparative Degree
degreeTypes.description: The Comparative Degree is the form of an adjective used to compare two people, things, or places and show that one has a greater or lesser quality than the other.
degreeTypes.urduExplanation: تقابلی درجہ صفت کی وہ صورت ہے جس کے ذریعے دو اشخاص، چیزوں یا جگہوں کے درمیان موازنہ کر کے یہ ظاہر کیا جاتا ہے کہ ایک میں کسی صفت کی مقدار دوسرے کے مقابلے میں زیادہ یا کم ہے۔
degreeTypes.exampleWords: Taller, cleverer, more intelligent, wider etc
rules: Compare two people, things, or places.
Use **than** after the comparative degree.
Use **more** with many longer adjectives.
Use **less** to show a lower degree.
Do not use a double comparative.
Use **than that of** when the compared singular noun is understood.
Use **those of** when the compared noun is plural.
ruleExamples:
Ali is **taller than** Ahmed.
Karachi is **larger than** Quetta.

She is **more intelligent than** her sister.
This book is **better than** that book.

**beautiful → more beautiful**
**important → more important**
**difficult → more difficult**

Ali is **less experienced than** Ahmed.
This road is **less crowded than** that road.

Incorrect: **more taller**
Correct: **taller**
The population of Karachi is greater than **that of** Quetta.
The natural **resources** of Pakistan are greater than **those of** many countries.

examples.text: Ali is **taller than** Ahmed.
examples.urdu: علی احمد سے زیادہ لمبا ہے۔
examples.note: **Taller than** compares two people, Ali and Ahmed, so the Comparative Degree is used.

examples.text: This question is **more difficult than** the previous one.
examples.urdu: یہ سوال پچھلے سوال سے زیادہ مشکل ہے۔
examples.note: **More difficult than** is used because **difficult** is a longer adjective and two questions are being compared.

examples.text: The population of Karachi is greater than **that of** Quetta.
examples.urdu: کراچی کی آبادی کوئٹہ کی آبادی سے زیادہ ہے۔
examples.note: **That of Quetta** replaces **the population of Quetta** and avoids repeating the singular noun **population**.

commonMistakes.urdu: علی احمد سے زیادہ لمبا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: **Taller** already contains the Comparative ending **-er**, so do not add **more**.

commonMistakes.right: This book is **better than** that one.
commonMistakes.urdu: یہ کتاب اس کتاب سے بہتر ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Use **than** after a comparative adjective; **that** alone is not the comparison marker.

commonMistakes.wrong: This road is **less crowded that** road.
commonMistakes.right: This road is **less crowded than** that road.
commonMistakes.urdu: یہ سڑک اس سڑک سے کم بھیڑ والی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: The lower degree uses **less + adjective + than** when comparing two roads.

commonMistakes.wrong: The population of Karachi is greater than **Quetta**.
commonMistakes.right: The population of Karachi is greater than **that of Quetta**.
commonMistakes.urdu: کراچی کی آبادی کوئٹہ کی آبادی سے زیادہ ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Use **that of** to represent the repeated singular noun **population**.

commonMistakes.wrong: Pakistan’s resources are greater than **that of** many countries.
commonMistakes.right: Pakistan’s resources are greater than **those of** many countries.
commonMistakes.urdu: پاکستان کے وسائل بہت سے ممالک کے وسائل سے زیادہ ہیں۔
commonMistakes.note: Use plural **those of** because **resources** is plural.

degreeTypes.name: Superlative Degree
degreeTypes.description: The Superlative Degree is the form of an adjective used to show the highest or lowest degree of a quality among three or more people, things, or places.
degreeTypes.urduExplanation: اعلیٰ ترین درجہ صفت کی وہ صورت ہے جس کے ذریعے تین یا تین سے زیادہ اشخاص، چیزوں یا جگہوں میں کسی صفت کی سب سے زیادہ یا سب سے کم مقدار ظاہر کی جاتی ہے۔
degreeTypes.exampleWords: Tallest, shortest, smartest, highest, most beautiful, most attractive
rules: Compare three or more people, things, or places.
Generally use **the** before the Superlative adjective.
Short adjectives usually take **-est**.
Use **most** with many longer adjectives.
Use **least** to show the lowest degree.
Use **in** or **of** to identify the group.
Do not use a double superlative.
ruleExamples:
Ali is **the tallest** boy in the class.
This is **the most expensive** car in the showroom.

She is **the smartest** student in the class.
He is **the best** player on the team.

**tall → tallest**
**small → smallest**
**fast → fastest**

**beautiful → most beautiful**
**important → most important**
**difficult → most difficult**

He is **the least experienced** member of the team.
This is **the least expensive** option.

He is the best student **in** the class.
He is the tallest **of** the three brothers.

Incorrect: **the most tallest**
Correct: **the tallest**

examples.text: Ali is **the tallest** boy in the class.
examples.urdu: علی جماعت کا سب سے لمبا لڑکا ہے۔
examples.note: **The tallest** compares Ali with three or more boys, so the Superlative Degree is used.

examples.text: This is **the most expensive** car in the showroom.
examples.urdu: یہ شوروم کی سب سے مہنگی گاڑی ہے۔
examples.note: **Most expensive** is used with the longer adjective **expensive**, and **the** comes before the superlative.

examples.text: He is **the tallest of** the three brothers.
examples.urdu: وہ تین بھائیوں میں سب سے لمبا ہے۔
examples.note: **Of the three brothers** identifies the group being compared, while **the tallest** shows the highest degree.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ali is **most tallest** boy in the class.
commonMistakes.right: Ali is **the tallest** boy in the class.
commonMistakes.urdu: علی جماعت کا سب سے لمبا لڑکا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Use **the** before a normal superlative and do not combine **most** with an adjective already ending in **-est**.

commonMistakes.wrong: This is **the more expensive** car in the showroom.
commonMistakes.right: This is **the most expensive** car in the showroom.
commonMistakes.urdu: یہ شوروم کی سب سے مہنگی گاڑی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: For a longer adjective compared with all cars, use **most**, not the Comparative word **more**.

commonMistakes.wrong: He is **the best student of** the class.
commonMistakes.right: He is **the best student in** the class.
commonMistakes.urdu: وہ جماعت کا بہترین طالب علم ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Use **in** commonly with a place or group such as a class.

commonMistakes.wrong: She is the tallest **in the three sisters**.
commonMistakes.right: She is the tallest **of the three sisters**.
commonMistakes.urdu: وہ تین بہنوں میں سب سے لمبی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Use **of** when the superlative is followed by a specific number of people or things.

commonMistakes.wrong: This is the **better answer of all**.
commonMistakes.right: This is the **best answer of all**.
commonMistakes.urdu: یہ سب میں بہترین جواب ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: When more than two answers are compared, use the Superlative form **best**, not the Comparative form **better**.

degreeTypes.name: Irregular Degrees Table
degreeTypes.description: Some adjectives do not form their comparative and superlative degrees by adding -er or -est. Memorize these important irregular forms for competitive examinations.
degreeTypes.urduExplanation: کچھ صفات کے تقابلی اور اعلیٰ ترین درجات عام اصول کے مطابق -er یا -est لگا کر نہیں بنتے۔ مسابقتی امتحانات کے لیے ان صورتوں کو یاد رکھنا ضروری ہے۔

examples.text: Sara is the **best** student in the class.
examples.urdu: سارہ جماعت کی بہترین طالبہ ہے۔
examples.note: **Best** is the irregular Superlative form of **good** because Sara is compared with all the students.

examples.text: Ahmed is **better** at mathematics than Ali.
examples.urdu: احمد علی کی نسبت ریاضی میں بہتر ہے۔
examples.note: **Better** is the irregular Comparative form of **good** and is followed by **than**.

examples.text: We need **further** information about the examination.
examples.urdu: ہمیں امتحان کے بارے میں مزید معلومات درکار ہیں۔
examples.note: **Further** is used here to mean additional information, not a physical distance.

commonMistakes.urdu: علی احمد سے بہتر ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: **Better** is already the Comparative form of **good**, so do not use **more** before it.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہ بہترین کھلاڑی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: **Best** is already the Superlative form, so do not add **most**.

commonMistakes.urdu: علی احمد سے بڑا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Use **older than** for a normal age comparison; **elder** is generally used before a family noun, such as elder brother.

commonMistakes.urdu: مجھے مزید وضاحت درکار ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Use **further** for additional information; **farther** usually refers to physical distance.

commonMistakes.wrong: This is the **latter** news report published today.
commonMistakes.right: This is the **latest** news report published today.
commonMistakes.urdu: یہ آج شائع ہونے والی تازہ ترین خبر ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Use **latest** for the newest item. **Latter** means the second of two previously mentioned items.

content.degreeNote:
Kinds of Adjective tell us what type of adjective it is.
Degrees of Comparison show the level of comparison of an adjective.

content.introduction: An adverb is a word that gives more information about a verb, adjective, another adverb, or a whole sentence.
content.urduExplanation: حرفِ حال وہ لفظ ہے جو کسی فعل، صفت، دوسرے حرفِ حال یا پورے جملے کے بارے میں مزید معلومات فراہم کرے۔
content.englishExplanation: Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs, answering questions like how, where, when, and how often. They add precision to our descriptions and help clarify the circumstances of an action or quality. While many adverbs end in -ly, some do not, and their placement in a sentence can vary depending on their type and the emphasis intended.

examples.text: The research team carefully analysed the survey data before presenting its findings.
examples.urdu: تحقیقی ٹیم نے اپنے نتائج پیش کرنے سے پہلے سروے کے اعداد و شمار کا احتیاط سے تجزیہ کیا۔
examples.note: 'Carefully' is an adverb of manner; it modifies 'analysed' and explains how the team performed the action.

examples.text: The committee will announce the final policy tomorrow after reviewing the public responses.
examples.urdu: کمیٹی عوامی آرا کا جائزہ لینے کے بعد کل حتمی پالیسی کا اعلان کرے گی۔
examples.note: 'Tomorrow' is an adverb of time; it specifies when the committee will announce the policy.

examples.text: The delegation met there to negotiate a peaceful solution to the regional dispute.
examples.urdu: وفد علاقائی تنازع کے پُرامن حل پر مذاکرات کرنے کے لیے وہاں ملا۔
examples.note: 'There' is an adverb of place; it identifies the location of the meeting and modifies 'met'.

examples.text: The candidate regularly reviews constitutional principles before attempting a difficult question.
examples.urdu: امیدوار مشکل سوال حل کرنے سے پہلے باقاعدگی سے آئینی اصولوں کا جائزہ لیتا ہے۔
examples.note: 'Regularly' is an adverb of frequency; it shows how often the candidate reviews the principles.

examples.text: The proposed reform is considerably more effective than the earlier administrative measure.
examples.urdu: مجوزہ اصلاح پہلے کے انتظامی اقدام سے خاصی زیادہ مؤثر ہے۔
examples.note: 'Considerably' is an adverb of degree; it intensifies the adjective 'more effective'.

examples.text: The witness explained the circumstances clearly, although the cross-examination was demanding.
examples.urdu: گواہ نے حالات کو واضح طور پر بیان کیا، اگرچہ جرح مشکل تھی۔
examples.note: 'Clearly' is an adverb of manner; it modifies 'explained' and describes the quality of the explanation.

examples.text: The institution rarely revises its examination policy without consulting experienced faculty members.
examples.urdu: ادارہ تجربہ کار اساتذہ سے مشورہ کیے بغیر شاذ و نادر ہی اپنی امتحانی پالیسی میں ترمیم کرتا ہے۔
examples.note: 'Rarely' is an adverb of frequency; it is placed before the main verb 'revises' to show how seldom the action occurs.

types.name: Adverb of Manner
types.description: An Adverb of Manner tells us how an action is performed.
types.urduExplanation: حرفِ حالِ طریقہ وہ لفظ ہے جو یہ بتاتا ہے کہ کوئی کام کس طرح یا کس انداز سے کیا گیا۔
types.exampleWords: slowly, quickly, carefully, politely, beautifully, loudly
rules: 1: It tells us how an action happens.
2: It usually modifies an action verb.
3: Many adverbs of manner are formed by adding **-ly** to an adjective.
4: Not every adverb of manner ends in **-ly**.
5: Be careful with adjectives and adverbs that look similar.
ruleExamples:
He speaks **politely**.
She writes **carefully**. > Test: Ask **"How?"** after the verb.

The boy ran **quickly**.
She answered **correctly**. > **Quickly** tells us how he ran, while **correctly** tells us how she answered.

careful → **carefully**
slow → **slowly**
quick → **quickly**
polite → **politely** > **Adjective + -ly → Adverb**.

He works **hard**.
She runs **fast**.
They arrived **late**. > **Hard**, **fast**, and **late** function as adverbs of manner.

❌ He runs **quick**.
✅ He runs **quickly**.
❌ She speaks **polite**.
✅ She speaks **politely**. > Use the adverb form for actions.

examples.text: He speaks **politely**.
examples.urdu: وہ شائستگی سے بولتا ہے۔
examples.note: **Politely** describes how he speaks.

examples.text: She writes **carefully**.
examples.urdu: وہ احتیاط سے لکھتی ہے۔
examples.note: **Carefully** describes how she writes.

examples.text: The boy ran **quickly**.
examples.urdu: لڑکا تیزی سے بھاگا۔
examples.note: **Quickly** describes how he ran.

examples.text: She answered **correctly**.
examples.urdu: اس نے صحیح جواب دیا۔
examples.note: **Correctly** tells us how she answered.

examples.text: He works **hard**.
examples.urdu: وہ سخت محنت کرتا ہے۔
examples.note: **Hard** is an adverb here.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہ تیزی سے بھاگتا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Use the adverb **quickly** to describe the action of running.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہ شائستگی سے بولتی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Use the adverb **politely** to describe how she speaks.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہ سخت محنت کرتا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: **Hardly** means 'almost not', while **hard** is the adverb for 'with effort'.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہ تیز بھاگتی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: **Fastly** is not a word; **fast** is both adjective and adverb.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہ خوبصورتی سے بولتا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Modify the verb with an adverb.

types.name: Adverb of Place
types.description: An Adverb of Place tells us where an action happens or where someone or something is located.
types.urduExplanation: حرفِ حالِ مکان وہ لفظ ہے جو یہ بتاتا ہے کہ کوئی کام کہاں ہوتا ہے یا کوئی شخص یا چیز کہاں موجود ہے۔
types.exampleWords: here, there, everywhere, outside, inside, nearby, abroad
rules: 1: It answers the question **"Where?"**.
2: It usually modifies a verb.
3: It can come before or after the verb depending on the sentence.
4: Some adverbs of place indicate direction or movement.
5: Do not confuse an adverb of place with a prepositional phrase.
ruleExamples:
Come **here**.
The children are playing **outside**. > Where should you come? → **Here**.

She looked **everywhere**.
He lives **nearby**. > **Everywhere** tells us where she looked.

Come **here**.
**Here** comes the bus.
The children are playing **outside**.
**Outside**, the weather is cold. > Positions are flexible.

The boy went **inside**.
She walked **away**.
The bird flew **upstairs**. > These tell us where someone moves.

He lives **here**. → **here** = adverb
He lives **in Quetta**. → **in Quetta** = prepositional phrase. > Adverbs of place can stand alone.

examples.text: Come **here**.
examples.urdu: یہاں آؤ۔
examples.note: **Here** is an adverb of place.

examples.text: The children are playing **outside**.
examples.urdu: بچے باہر کھیل رہے ہیں۔
examples.note: **Outside** tells us where they are playing.

examples.text: She looked **everywhere**.
examples.urdu: اس نے ہر جگہ دیکھا۔
examples.note: **Everywhere** is an adverb of place.

examples.text: He lives **nearby**.
examples.urdu: وہ قریب ہی رہتا ہے۔
examples.note: **Nearby** tells us where he lives.

examples.text: The boy went **inside**.
examples.urdu: لڑکا اندر چلا گیا۔
examples.note: **Inside** indicates the direction.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہ یہاں رہتا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: **Here** is an adverb and does not need a preposition like **in**.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہ بیرون ملک چلی گئی۔
commonMistakes.note: **Abroad** is an adverb, so we don't use 'to' before it.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہاں جاؤ۔
commonMistakes.note: Don't use 'to' with the adverb **there**.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہ باہر ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: **Outside** functions as an adverb here.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہ اوپر ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: **Upstairs** does not need the preposition 'at'.

types.name: Adverb of Time
types.description: An Adverb of Time tells us when an action happens, happened, or will happen.
types.urduExplanation: حرفِ حالِ زمان وہ لفظ ہے جو یہ بتاتا ہے کہ کوئی کام کب ہوتا ہے، ہوا، یا ہوگا۔
types.exampleWords: now, today, yesterday, tomorrow, soon, later, already, recently
rules: 1: It answers **"When?"**.
2: It usually modifies a verb or the action of the sentence.
3: Adverbs of time can occur at the beginning or end of a sentence.
4: Some adverbs of time show a specific time.
5: Some adverbs of time show an indefinite time.
6: Do not confuse **ago** and **before**.
ruleExamples:
He arrived **yesterday**.
I will call you **tomorrow**. > When did he arrive? → **Yesterday**.

She finished her work **early**.
They arrived **late**. > **Early** tells us when she finished.

**Today**, I am studying English.
I am studying English **today**. > Position can change.

He came **yesterday**.
We will leave **tomorrow**. > These identify a particular time.

She has **already** finished her work.
He will arrive **soon**. > These indicate time without giving an exact time.

He left two days **ago**.
I had seen him **before**. > **Ago** is for time from now; **before** is for time earlier than another point.

examples.text: He arrived **yesterday**.
examples.urdu: وہ کل پہنچا۔
examples.note: **Yesterday** is an adverb of time.

examples.text: I will call you **tomorrow**.
examples.urdu: میں آپ کو کل فون کروں گا۔
examples.note: **Tomorrow** tells us when.

types.name: Adverb of Frequency
types.description: An Adverb of Frequency tells us how often an action happens.
types.urduExplanation: حرفِ حالِ تکرار وہ لفظ ہے جو یہ بتاتا ہے کہ کوئی کام کتنی بار یا کتنی کثرت سے ہوتا ہے۔
types.exampleWords: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, seldom, never
rules: 1: It answers **"How often?"**.
2: Adverbs of frequency usually come before the main verb.
3: With the verb **to be**, the adverb usually comes after **be**.
4: With auxiliary or modal verbs, the adverb usually comes after the first auxiliary/modal.
5: **Never** already has a negative meaning.
6: Frequency adverbs can indicate different levels of frequency.
ruleExamples:
He **always** studies.
She **often** reads newspapers. > How often does he study? → **Always**.

He **always** works hard.
They **often** visit us. > **Subject + frequency adverb + main verb**.

He is **always** punctual.
She is **never** late. > **Subject + be + frequency adverb**.

She has **always** worked hard.
He can **often** help us. > After the first auxiliary/modal.

He **never** lies. ✅
❌ He doesn't **never** lie. > Avoid double negatives.

High: **always, usually, often**
Low: **sometimes, occasionally, rarely, seldom**
Zero: **never**.

types.name: Adverb of Degree
types.description: An Adverb of Degree tells us the intensity or extent of an action, adjective, or another adverb.
types.urduExplanation: حرفِ حالِ مقدار یا شدت وہ لفظ ہے جو کسی فعل، صفت یا دوسرے حرفِ حال کی مقدار، شدت یا درجے کو ظاہر کرے۔
types.exampleWords: very, too, quite, extremely, almost, enough, completely, rather
rules: 1: It answers **"To what extent?"** or **"How much?"**.
2: It can modify an adjective.
3: It can modify another adverb.
4: Some adverbs of degree can modify verbs.
5: Do not confuse **very** and **too**.
6: **Enough** usually comes after an adjective or adverb, but before a noun.
ruleExamples:
She is **very** intelligent.
He was **extremely** tired. > How intelligent? → **Very**. To what extent tired? → **Extremely**.

The exam was **very** difficult.
She is **extremely** intelligent. > **Adverb of Degree + Adjective**.

He runs **very** quickly.
She speaks **quite** slowly. > **Very** modifies quickly, while **quite** modifies slowly.

I **completely** agree with you.
She **almost** fell. > **Completely** shows the extent of agree, while **almost** shows proximity.

The bag is **very** heavy. (Highly heavy)
The bag is **too** heavy to carry. (Excessively heavy) > **Very** increases intensity; **too** indicates excess.

The room is large **enough**.
He runs quickly **enough**.
We have **enough** food. > **Adjective/Adverb + enough**; **Enough + noun**.

types.name: Adverb of Affirmation and Negation
types.description: An Adverb of Affirmation expresses agreement, certainty, or confirmation, while an Adverb of Negation expresses denial or refusal.
types.urduExplanation: حرفِ حالِ اثبات و نفی وہ لفظ ہے جو کسی بات کے یقینی، درست یا تسلیم شدہ ہونے یا اس کے انکار یا نفی کو ظاہر کرے۔
types.exampleWords: certainly, surely, definitely, indeed, not, never, nowhere, hardly
rules: 1: Adverbs of affirmation show certainty or confirmation.
2: Adverbs of negation make a statement negative.
3: **Not** usually comes after an auxiliary or helping verb.
4: **Never** means **"at no time"** and already carries a negative meaning.
5: Do not use two negatives to express one negative idea.
6: Some adverbs can strongly emphasize certainty.
ruleExamples:
He will **certainly** succeed.
She is **definitely** coming. > These show confidence in the truth.

He is **not** ready.
She **never** lies. > These deny or negate the statement.

He is **not** ready.
They do **not** agree.
She has **not** finished. > **Auxiliary verb + not + main verb**.

He **never** wastes his time.
She **never** misses her class. > ❌ He doesn't **never** study. ✅ He **never** studies.

❌ I don't know **nothing**.
✅ I don't know **anything**. OR ✅ I know **nothing**. > Avoid double negatives.

He will **definitely** pass.
She has **certainly** worked hard. > These strengthen the speaker's certainty.

types.name: Interrogative Adverb
types.description: An Interrogative Adverb is a word used to ask questions about the time, place, manner, or reason of an action.
types.urduExplanation: حرفِ حالِ استفہام وہ لفظ ہے جو کسی کام کے وقت، جگہ، طریقے یا وجہ کے بارے میں سوال پوچھنے کے لیے استعمال ہوتا ہے۔
types.exampleWords: when, where, why, how
rules: 1: **When** asks about time.
2: **Where** asks about place.
3: **Why** asks about reason or cause.
4: **How** asks about manner or method.
5: An interrogative adverb is used to form a question.
6: Do not confuse an interrogative adverb with an interrogative adjective.
ruleExamples:
**When** will you arrive?
**When** did he leave? > Asks at what time.

**Where** do you live?
**Where** did they go? > Asks at what place.

**Why** are you late?
**Why** did she leave? > Asks for the reason.

**How** did you solve the problem?
**How** does he work? > Asks in what way.

**When** will the exam begin?
**Where** is your college? > Introduces a question.

**How** did you solve the problem? (**How** = Adverb)
**Which** book did you read? (**Which** = Adjective) > Adjectives modify nouns.

commonMistakes.note: Use **how** for manner, not **which** (unless referring to a specific item).

types.name: Relative Adverb
types.description: A Relative Adverb is a word that connects a clause to a noun or idea mentioned earlier and gives information about place, time, or reason.
types.urduExplanation: حرفِ حالِ موصولہ وہ لفظ ہے جو کسی پہلے بیان کیے گئے اسم یا خیال کو ایک تابع جملے سے جوڑتا ہے اور جگہ، وقت یا وجہ کے بارے میں معلومات دیتا ہے۔
types.exampleWords: where, when, why
rules: 1: **Where** refers to a place.
2: **When** refers to a time.
3: **Why** refers to a reason.
4: A relative adverb connects two parts of a sentence.
5: Do not confuse a relative adverb with an interrogative adverb.
ruleExamples: This is the place **where** I was born. > Connects clause with the noun 'place'.
I remember the day **when** we first met. > Connects clause with the noun 'day'.
I know the reason **why** he left. > Connects clause with the noun 'reason'.

This is the house **where** Ali lives.
I remember the year **when** Pakistan was created. > Acts as a link.

Interrogative: **Where** do you live? (Asks a question)
Relative: This is the city **where** I live. (Connects clauses) > Check for question mark vs. connection.

types.name: Conjunctive Adverb
types.description: A Conjunctive Adverb is a word or phrase that connects two ideas or clauses and shows their relationship, such as contrast, result, addition, or sequence.
types.urduExplanation: حرفِ حالِ رابط وہ لفظ یا فقرہ ہے جو دو خیالات یا جملوں کو آپس میں جوڑتا ہے اور ان کے درمیان تعلق، جیسے اختلاف، نتیجہ، اضافہ یا ترتیب، ظاہر کرتا ہے۔
types.exampleWords: however, therefore, moreover, nevertheless, consequently, otherwise
rules: 1: It connects two related ideas or clauses.
2: It can show contrast.
3: It can show result or consequence.
4: It can show addition.
5: Pay attention to punctuation.
6: Do not confuse a conjunctive adverb with a coordinating conjunction.
ruleExamples:
He worked hard; **therefore**, he passed.
She was tired; **however**, she continued studying. > Shows result and contrast.
He is poor; **however**, he is honest. > Words like **however**, **nevertheless** show contrast.
It was raining; **therefore**, we stayed home. > Words like **therefore**, **consequently** show a result.
He is intelligent; **moreover**, he is hardworking. > Words like **moreover**, **furthermore** add ideas.

He was tired; **however**, he continued working.
He was tired. **However**, he continued working. > Use a semicolon or full stop before, and a comma after.

He was tired, **but** he continued working. (**but** = conjunction)
He was tired; **however**, he continued working. (**however** = conjunctive adverb) > **but** directly joins; **however** shows relationship.

examples.note: **Therefore** shows the result.

examples.note: **Therefore** shows consequence.

commonMistakes.note: Conjunctive adverbs need proper punctuation (semicolon and comma).

commonMistakes.note: A comma alone (comma splice) is incorrect before a conjunctive adverb.

commonMistakes.note: Do not use a coordinating conjunction (**but**) and a conjunctive adverb (**however**) together.

commonMistakes.note: Missing punctuation makes the sentence hard to read.

commonMistakes.note: Use a semicolon before **consequently** when joining two independent clauses.

types.name: Adverb of Reason/Result
types.description: An Adverb of Reason/Result shows the reason, result, or consequence of an action or situation.
types.urduExplanation: حرفِ حالِ وجہ/نتیجہ وہ لفظ ہے جو کسی کام یا صورتِ حال کی وجہ یا اس کے نتیجے کو ظاہر کرے۔
types.exampleWords: therefore, hence, thus, consequently, accordingly
rules: 1: It shows a result or consequence.
2: It can show the result of a previous statement.
3: **Therefore** means **"for that reason"** or **"as a result."**
4: **Hence** can mean **"therefore"** or **"for this reason."**
5: Do not confuse reason with result.
ruleExamples: He worked hard; **therefore**, he succeeded. > Shows the result of working hard.
The road was blocked; **consequently**, we took another route. > Introduces the result of the blocked road.
He was ill; **therefore**, he could not attend the class. > Use when the second idea is the logical result.
He was the senior officer; **hence**, he made the final decision. > Introduces the result or conclusion.

He was ill **because** he had a fever. (**because** = reason)
He had a fever; **therefore**, he stayed home. (**therefore** = result) > **Because** gives reason; **Therefore** gives result.

examples.text: He worked hard; **therefore**, he succeeded.
examples.urdu: اس نے سخت محنت کی، اس لیے وہ کامیاب ہو گیا۔
examples.note: **Therefore** shows the result.

examples.text: The road was blocked; **consequently**, we took another route.
examples.urdu: سڑک بند تھی، نتیجتاً ہم نے دوسرا راستہ اختیار کیا۔

examples.text: He was ill; **therefore**, he could not attend the class.

examples.text: He was the senior officer; **hence**, he made the final decision.
examples.urdu: وہ سینئر افسر تھا، اس لیے اس نے حتمی فیصلہ کیا۔
examples.note: **Hence** introduces the conclusion.

examples.text: It was late; **thus**, we decided to leave.
examples.urdu: دیر ہو چکی تھی، اس لیے ہم نے جانے کا فیصلہ کیا۔
examples.note: **Thus** indicates the result.

commonMistakes.wrong: He stayed home **because** he was ill. (when you mean result)
commonMistakes.right: He was ill; **therefore**, he stayed home.
commonMistakes.urdu: وہ بیمار تھا، اس لیے وہ گھر پر رہا۔
commonMistakes.note: Use **therefore** for the result, not **because**.

commonMistakes.urdu: اس نے سخت محنت کی، اس لیے وہ پاس ہو گیا۔
commonMistakes.note: Use proper punctuation with adverbs of result.

commonMistakes.wrong: He is rich **therefore** he is happy. (without punctuation)
commonMistakes.right: He is rich; **therefore**, he is happy.
commonMistakes.urdu: وہ امیر ہے، اس لیے وہ خوش ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Semicolon and comma are needed for clarity.

commonMistakes.urdu: میں بھوکا تھا، نتیجتاً میں نے کھایا۔
commonMistakes.note: Punctuation helps separate the two independent clauses.

commonMistakes.wrong: He lied **therefore** I am angry. (missing punctuation)
commonMistakes.urdu: اس نے جھوٹ بولا، اس لیے میں ناراض ہوں۔
commonMistakes.note: Use a semicolon before the result adverb.

rules: Adverbs of manner are usually placed after the main verb or after the object if there is one (She sings beautifully).
Adverbs of frequency are placed before the main verb but after auxiliary verbs and the verb 'to be' (He always arrives on time; She is often late).
Adverbs of time are typically placed at the beginning or end of a sentence, not in the middle (Yesterday, I finished my homework).
Do not confuse adjectives and adverbs; adjectives describe nouns while adverbs describe verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs (She is a careful driver vs. She drives carefully).
Some words ending in -ly, like friendly and lovely, are actually adjectives, not adverbs, so check meaning carefully.
Adverbs of degree usually appear directly before the adjective or adverb they modify (The exam was extremely difficult).

commonMistakes.wrong: The committee reviewed the proposal careful before approving it.
commonMistakes.right: The committee reviewed the proposal carefully before approving it.
commonMistakes.urdu: کمیٹی نے منظوری دینے سے پہلے تجویز کا احتیاط سے جائزہ لیا۔
commonMistakes.note: 'Carefully' is required because it modifies the verb 'reviewed'; 'careful' is an adjective and cannot modify this verb.

commonMistakes.wrong: The analyst explained the statistical results clear to the panel.
commonMistakes.right: The analyst explained the statistical results clearly to the panel.
commonMistakes.urdu: تجزیہ کار نے شماریاتی نتائج پینل کو واضح طور پر سمجھائے۔
commonMistakes.note: 'Clearly' is the adverbial form needed to modify 'explained'; 'clear' is an adjective.

commonMistakes.wrong: The government always has responded promptly to such emergencies.
commonMistakes.right: The government has always responded promptly to such emergencies.
commonMistakes.urdu: حکومت نے ہمیشہ ایسی ہنگامی صورتِ حال پر فوری ردِعمل دیا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: With an auxiliary verb such as 'has', the frequency adverb normally comes after the auxiliary and before the past participle.

commonMistakes.wrong: The report was extremely well-researched, but the conclusion was surprising enough.
commonMistakes.right: The report was extremely well-researched, but the conclusion was surprisingly weak.
commonMistakes.urdu: رپورٹ کا تحقیقی کام نہایت عمدہ تھا، لیکن نتیجہ حیرت انگیز طور پر کمزور تھا۔
commonMistakes.note: 'Surprisingly' modifies the adjective 'weak'; 'surprising' describes a noun or subject rather than the manner or degree of the conclusion.

commonMistakes.wrong: The senior researcher spoke friendly to the participants during the interview.
commonMistakes.right: The senior researcher spoke in a friendly manner to the participants during the interview.
commonMistakes.urdu: سینئر محقق نے انٹرویو کے دوران شرکا سے دوستانہ انداز میں بات کی۔
commonMistakes.note: 'Friendly' is an adjective, not a standard adverb; the phrase 'in a friendly manner' correctly modifies the verb 'spoke'.

content.introduction: A conjunction is a word that connects words, phrases, or clauses in a sentence.
content.urduExplanation: حرفِ عطف وہ لفظ ہے جو جملے میں الفاظ، فقروں یا جملوں کے حصوں کو آپس میں جوڑتا ہے۔
content.englishExplanation: Conjunctions are the 'glue' of language. They allow us to form complex sentences by linking different ideas together. There are three main types: Coordinating (joining equal parts), Subordinating (joining dependent parts to independent ones), and Correlative (working in pairs). Proper use of conjunctions is vital for cohesion and flow in writing, especially in formal essays and competitive examinations.

examples.text: and, but, or, so, because, although, if, either...or, neither...nor
examples.note: Common examples of conjunctions.

types.name: Coordinating Conjunctions
types.description: Coordinating conjunctions connect words, phrases, or independent clauses of equal grammatical importance.
types.urduExplanation: ہم رتبہ حروفِ عطف وہ الفاظ ہیں جو برابر کی گرامر کی اہمیت رکھنے والے الفاظ، فقروں یا آزاد جملوں کو آپس میں جوڑتے ہیں۔
types.exampleWords: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so (FANBOYS)
rules: 1: Use **and** to add one thing to another.
2: Use **but** to show contrast or difference.
3: Use **or** to show a choice or alternative.
4: Use **so** to show a result or consequence.
5: Use **for** to show a reason (similar to because).
6: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction when it joins two independent clauses.
ruleExamples:
I like tea **and** coffee.
He bought a pen **and** a notebook. > Addition: **and**.

He is poor **but** honest.
I wanted to go, **but** it was raining. > Contrast: **but**.

Do you want tea **or** coffee?
You can go by bus **or** by train. > Choice: **or**.

He was tired, **so** he went to sleep.
It was raining, **so** we stayed home. > Result: **so**.

He was happy, **for** he had passed the exam.
I believed him, **for** he had never lied. > Reason: **for**.

She is intelligent, **and** she is also very kind.
He worked hard, **but** he failed. > Punctuation rule.

examples.text: I like tea **and** coffee.
examples.urdu: مجھے چائے اور کافی پسند ہے۔
examples.note: **And** connects two similar things.

examples.text: He is poor **but** honest.
examples.urdu: وہ غریب ہے لیکن ایماندار ہے۔
examples.note: **But** shows contrast.

examples.text: Do you want tea **or** coffee?
examples.urdu: کیا آپ چائے چاہتے ہیں یا کافی؟
examples.note: **Or** shows a choice.

examples.text: He was tired, **so** he went to sleep.
examples.urdu: وہ تھکا ہوا تھا، اس لیے وہ سو گیا۔
examples.note: **So** shows the result.

examples.text: She is intelligent, **yet** she is very humble.
examples.urdu: وہ ذہین ہے، پھر بھی وہ بہت عاجز ہے۔
examples.note: **Yet** shows contrast like but.

commonMistakes.wrong: He is poor **and** honest. (when you want to show contrast)
commonMistakes.urdu: وہ غریب ہے لیکن ایماندار ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Use **but** to show the contrast between being poor and honest.

commonMistakes.wrong: I will go, **or** I will stay. (without a comma joining long clauses)
commonMistakes.right: I will go, **or** I will stay.
commonMistakes.urdu: میں جاؤں گا، یا میں رکوں گا۔
commonMistakes.note: Always use a comma when joining two full sentences.

commonMistakes.wrong: He worked hard **so** he passed. (without comma)
commonMistakes.urdu: اس نے سخت محنت کی، اس لیے وہ پاس ہو گیا۔
commonMistakes.note: Use a comma before **so** when it connects two clauses.

commonMistakes.urdu: کیا آپ چائے چاہتے ہیں یا کافی؟
commonMistakes.note: Use **or** for choices, not **but**.

commonMistakes.wrong: He was late **for** he missed the bus. (without comma)
commonMistakes.right: He was late, **for** he missed the bus.
commonMistakes.urdu: اسے دیر ہو گئی کیونکہ اس کی بس چھوٹ گئی تھی۔
commonMistakes.note: When **for** means because, use a comma before it.

types.name: Subordinating Conjunctions
types.description: Subordinating conjunctions connect a dependent (subordinate) clause to an independent clause.
types.urduExplanation: ماتحت حروفِ عطف وہ الفاظ ہیں جو ایک تابع جملے کو ایک آزاد جملے سے جوڑتے ہیں۔
types.exampleWords: because, although, if, since, while, unless, until, after, before
rules: 1: Use **because** to show a reason.
2: Use **although** or **though** to show contrast or concession.
3: Use **if** or **unless** to show a condition.
4: Use **since** to show a reason or a point in time.
5: Use **while** or **as** to show actions happening at the same time.
6: If the subordinating conjunction starts the sentence, use a comma after the dependent clause.
ruleExamples:
I stayed home **because** it was raining.
She cried **because** she was sad. > Reason: **because**.

**Although** he is rich, he is unhappy.
He went out **though** it was cold. > Contrast: **although/though**.

I will go **if** you come.
You will fail **unless** you work hard. > Condition: **if/unless**.

I have been here **since** morning.
**Since** you are here, let's start. > Reason/Time: **since**.

I saw him **while** I was walking.
She sang **as** she worked. > Simultaneous actions: **while/as**.

**Because** it was raining, I stayed home.
**If** you work hard, you will pass. > Punctuation rule.

examples.text: I stayed home **because** it was raining.
examples.urdu: میں گھر پر رہا کیونکہ بارش ہو رہی تھی۔
examples.note: **Because** introduces the reason.

examples.text: **Although** he is rich, he is unhappy.
examples.urdu: اگرچہ وہ امیر ہے، وہ ناخوش ہے۔
examples.note: **Although** shows contrast.

examples.text: I will go **if** you come.
examples.urdu: اگر تم آؤ گے تو میں جاؤں گا۔
examples.note: **If** shows a condition.

examples.text: You will fail **unless** you work hard.
examples.urdu: تم ناکام ہو جاؤ گے جب تک کہ تم محنت نہیں کرو گے۔
examples.note: **Unless** means 'if not'.

examples.text: I saw him **while** I was walking.
examples.urdu: میں نے اسے دیکھا جب میں چل رہا تھا۔
examples.note: **While** shows time.

commonMistakes.wrong: **Although** he is poor **but** he is honest.
commonMistakes.right: **Although** he is poor, he is honest. (OR He is poor **but** he is honest.)
commonMistakes.urdu: اگرچہ وہ غریب ہے، وہ ایماندار ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Do not use **although** and **but** in the same sentence.

commonMistakes.wrong: **Because** he was ill **so** he stayed home.
commonMistakes.right: **Because** he was ill, he stayed home. (OR He was ill, **so** he stayed home.)
commonMistakes.urdu: چونکہ وہ بیمار تھا، وہ گھر پر رہا۔
commonMistakes.note: Do not use **because** and **so** together.

commonMistakes.wrong: I will not go **if** you **will** not come.
commonMistakes.right: I will not go **if** you **do** not come.
commonMistakes.urdu: اگر تم نہیں آؤ گے تو میں نہیں جاؤں گا۔
commonMistakes.note: Do not use 'will' in the if-clause for future conditions.

commonMistakes.urdu: یہاں انتظار کرو جب تک میں واپس نہ آ جاؤں۔
commonMistakes.note: **Until** already has a negative meaning; don't use 'not' with it.

commonMistakes.wrong: **Unless** you **don't** work hard, you will fail.
commonMistakes.right: **Unless** you work hard, you will fail.
commonMistakes.urdu: جب تک تم محنت نہیں کرو گے، تم ناکام ہو جاؤ گے۔
commonMistakes.note: **Unless** means 'if not', so don't add another 'not'.

types.name: Correlative Conjunctions
types.description: Correlative conjunctions are pairs of words that work together to connect balanced parts of a sentence.
types.urduExplanation: لازمی جوڑی دار حروفِ عطف وہ الفاظ کے جوڑے ہیں جو جملے کے متوازن حصوں کو جوڑنے کے لیے مل کر کام کرتے ہیں۔
types.exampleWords: either...or, neither...nor, both...and, not only...but also, whether...or
rules: 1: Use **either...or** to show a choice between two things.
2: Use **neither...nor** to reject both options.
3: Use **both...and** to include two things or people.
4: Use **not only...but also** to emphasize that two things are true.
5: Ensure parallel structure (use the same grammatical form after both parts of the pair).
6: When joining subjects, the verb usually agrees with the closer subject.
ruleExamples:
You can **either** stay **or** leave.
**Either** Ali **or** his friends are coming. > Choice: **either...or**.

**Neither** Ali **nor** Ahmed is present.
I like **neither** tea **nor** coffee. > Rejection: **neither...nor**.

**Both** Ali **and** Ahmed are coming.
He is **both** intelligent **and** hardworking. > Inclusion: **both...and**.

He is **not only** intelligent **but also** kind.
She **not only** sings **but also** dances. > Emphasis: **not only...but also**.
❌ He is **either** intelligent **or** a fool. ✅ He is **either** intelligent **or** foolish. > Parallelism: Use two adjectives.

**Neither** the teacher **nor** the students **are** here.
**Neither** the students **nor** the teacher **is** here. > Verb agreement.

examples.text: You can **either** stay **or** leave.
examples.urdu: آپ یا تو رک سکتے ہیں یا جا سکتے ہیں۔
examples.note: **Either...or** shows a choice.

examples.text: **Neither** Ali **nor** Ahmed is present.
examples.urdu: نہ علی اور نہ ہی احمد حاضر ہے۔
examples.note: **Neither...nor** negates both.

examples.text: **Both** Ali **and** Ahmed are coming.
examples.urdu: علی اور احمد دونوں آ رہے ہیں۔
examples.note: **Both...and** includes both.

examples.text: He is **not only** intelligent **but also** kind.
examples.urdu: وہ نہ صرف ذہین ہے بلکہ مہربان بھی ہے۔
examples.note: **Not only...but also** adds emphasis.

examples.text: **Whether** you like it **or** not, you have to do it.
examples.urdu: چاہے آپ کو پسند ہو یا نہ ہو، آپ کو یہ کرنا پڑے گا۔
examples.note: **Whether...or** shows two possibilities.

commonMistakes.urdu: نہ علی اور نہ احمد یہاں ہیں۔
commonMistakes.note: Always pair **neither** with **nor**, not **or**.

commonMistakes.urdu: یا تو تم رکو یا تم جاؤ۔
commonMistakes.note: Always pair **either** with **or**, not **nor**.

commonMistakes.wrong: He is **not only** a singer **but** a dancer.
commonMistakes.right: He is **not only** a singer **but also** a dancer.
commonMistakes.urdu: وہ نہ صرف ایک گلوکار ہے بلکہ ایک ڈانسر بھی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Don't forget the **also** in **not only...but also**.

commonMistakes.urdu: علی اور احمد دونوں آئے۔
commonMistakes.note: Always pair **both** with **and**, not **as well as**.

commonMistakes.right: He likes **neither** to swim **nor** to run (OR **neither** swimming **nor** running).
commonMistakes.urdu: اسے نہ تیرنا پسند ہے اور نہ ہی دوڑنا۔
commonMistakes.note: Maintain parallel structure (infinitive with infinitive, or gerund with gerund).

types.name: Conjunctive Adverbs
types.description: Conjunctive adverbs connect ideas by showing a logical relationship such as contrast, result, addition, sequence, or alternative. They are adverbs, not coordinating conjunctions.
types.urduExplanation: Conjunctive Adverbs ایسے ظروف ہیں جو دو خیالات یا آزاد جملوں کے درمیان منطقی تعلق ظاہر کرتے ہیں، جیسے مخالفت، نتیجہ، اضافہ، ترتیب یا متبادل۔ یہ حروفِ عطف نہیں بلکہ قید کی ایک قسم ہیں۔
types.wordFocus: however, therefore, moreover, furthermore, consequently, nevertheless, otherwise, meanwhile, similarly, indeed

cells: He was tired; however, he continued working.
It rained heavily; therefore, the match was postponed.
She is honest; moreover, she is hardworking.
Hurry up; otherwise, you will miss the bus.
The committee met; meanwhile, the secretary prepared the report.
He is indeed a capable officer.

examples.text: The road was blocked; **however,** we found another route.
examples.urdu: سڑک بند تھی؛ تاہم، ہمیں ایک دوسرا راستہ مل گیا۔
examples.note: **However** shows contrast between two independent clauses.

examples.text: She worked consistently; **therefore,** she secured the highest marks.
examples.urdu: اس نے مستقل مزاجی سے محنت کی؛ لہٰذا، اس نے سب سے زیادہ نمبر حاصل کیے۔
examples.note: **Therefore** introduces a result.

examples.text: The proposal is practical; **moreover,** it is affordable.
examples.urdu: یہ تجویز عملی ہے؛ مزید یہ کہ یہ کم خرچ بھی ہے۔
examples.note: **Moreover** adds a stronger supporting point.

examples.text: You must submit the form today; **otherwise,** your application will be rejected.
examples.urdu: آپ کو آج فارم جمع کرانا ہوگا؛ بصورتِ دیگر، آپ کی درخواست مسترد کر دی جائے گی۔
examples.note: **Otherwise** presents an alternative consequence.

examples.text: The principal addressed the students; **meanwhile,** the teachers arranged the examination hall.
examples.urdu: پرنسپل نے طلبہ سے خطاب کیا؛ اسی دوران، اساتذہ نے امتحانی ہال کا انتظام کیا۔
examples.note: **Meanwhile** shows simultaneous time.

examples.text: The evidence was **indeed** sufficient to support the argument.
examples.urdu: ثبوت واقعی دلیل کی حمایت کے لیے کافی تھا۔
examples.note: **Indeed** adds emphasis.

examples.text: The first method is costly; **similarly,** the second method requires special equipment.
examples.urdu: پہلا طریقہ مہنگا ہے؛ اسی طرح، دوسرے طریقے کے لیے خصوصی آلات درکار ہیں۔
examples.note: **Similarly** introduces a comparable point.

rules: A conjunctive adverb is an adverbial connector; it is not one of the coordinating conjunctions in FANBOYS.
When it joins two independent clauses, place a semicolon before it and usually a comma after it: Clause; however, clause.
A full stop may replace the semicolon: Clause. However, clause.
Do not join two independent clauses with only a comma before a conjunctive adverb; that creates a comma splice.
Use a comma when a conjunctive adverb interrupts one independent clause: The answer is, therefore, correct.
Choose the adverb according to the intended relationship: however for contrast, therefore for result, and moreover for addition.
ruleExamples: He was poor; however, he was honest.
He was poor. However, he was honest.
The evidence was incomplete; therefore, the judge postponed the decision.
Incorrect: He was poor, however he was honest. Correct: He was poor; however, he was honest.
The plan is, moreover, financially sound.
The machine failed; consequently, production stopped.

commonMistakes.wrong: He was tired, however he continued working.
commonMistakes.right: He was tired; however, he continued working.
commonMistakes.urdu: وہ تھکا ہوا تھا؛ تاہم، وہ کام کرتا رہا۔
commonMistakes.note: Do not use only a comma to join two independent clauses.

commonMistakes.wrong: It was raining, therefore the match was cancelled.
commonMistakes.right: It was raining; therefore, the match was cancelled.
commonMistakes.urdu: بارش ہو رہی تھی؛ لہٰذا، میچ منسوخ کر دیا گیا۔
commonMistakes.note: Use a semicolon before **therefore** when it joins complete clauses.

commonMistakes.wrong: Although he was ill; however, he attended the exam.
commonMistakes.right: Although he was ill, he attended the exam.
commonMistakes.urdu: اگرچہ وہ بیمار تھا، پھر بھی وہ امتحان میں شریک ہوا۔
commonMistakes.note: Do not unnecessarily combine **although** with **however** in the same structure.

commonMistakes.wrong: He did not study; moreover he failed.
commonMistakes.right: He did not study; moreover, he failed.
commonMistakes.urdu: اس نے مطالعہ نہیں کیا؛ مزید یہ کہ وہ ناکام ہو گیا۔
commonMistakes.note: Use a comma after a conjunctive adverb placed between clauses.

commonMistakes.wrong: She is however capable of doing the work.
commonMistakes.right: She is, however, capable of doing the work.
commonMistakes.urdu: تاہم، وہ یہ کام کرنے کی اہل ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: An interrupting conjunctive adverb is normally set off with commas.

commonMistakes.wrong: He worked hard, therefore he passed.
commonMistakes.right: He worked hard; therefore, he passed.
commonMistakes.urdu: اس نے سخت محنت کی؛ لہٰذا، وہ کامیاب ہو گیا۔
commonMistakes.note: A comma splice is incorrect between two independent clauses.

commonMistakes.wrong: The first answer is correct; otherwise, the second answer is also correct.
commonMistakes.right: The first answer is correct; similarly, the second answer is also correct.
commonMistakes.urdu: پہلا جواب درست ہے؛ اسی طرح، دوسرا جواب بھی درست ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Use **similarly** for similarity and **otherwise** for an alternative or negative consequence.

content.introduction: A determiner is a word placed before a noun to clarify what the noun refers to, indicating specificity, quantity, or possession.
content.urduExplanation: حرفِ تعین وہ لفظ ہے جو کسی اسم سے پہلے آ کر یہ واضح کرتا ہے کہ وہ اسم کس چیز، کتنی مقدار یا کس کی ملکیت کی طرف اشارہ کر رہا ہے۔
content.englishExplanation: Determiners are essential for defining nouns. They help the reader understand if we are talking about something specific (the book) or general (a book), how many things we are talking about (some books), or who owns them (my books). In competitive exams, the correct use of determiners—especially articles and quantifiers—is a key marker of advanced English proficiency.

examples.text: a, an, the, this, that, my, your, some, any, each, every, which
examples.note: Common examples of determiners.

types.name: Articles
types.description: Articles are the most common determiners. They indicate whether a noun is specific or general.
types.urduExplanation: آرٹیکلز سب سے زیادہ استعمال ہونے والے ڈٹرمینرز ہیں۔ یہ بتاتے ہیں کہ کوئی اسم خاص ہے یا عام۔
types.exampleWords: a, an, the
rules: 1: Use **a** before singular countable nouns starting with a consonant sound.
2: Use **an** before singular countable nouns starting with a vowel sound.
3: Use **the** for specific nouns that the listener already knows about.
4: Use **the** for unique things (e.g., the sun, the sky).
5: Use **the** before superlative adjectives (e.g., the best, the tallest).
6: Do not use **a/an** with uncountable nouns.
ruleExamples:
I have **a** book.
He is **a** doctor. > Consonant sound: **a**.

She ate **an** apple.
He is **an** honest man. > Vowel sound: **an**.

I saw a movie. **The** movie was great.
Open **the** door. > Specific/Previously mentioned: **the**.

**The** sun rises in the east.
**The** earth is round. > Unique things: **the**.

He is **the** best student in the class.
This is **the** most beautiful flower. > Superlatives: **the**.
❌ I need **a** water. ✅ I need **some** water. > Uncountable nouns rule.

examples.text: I have **a** book.
examples.urdu: میرے پاس ایک کتاب ہے۔
examples.note: **A** is used for a non-specific singular noun.

examples.text: She ate **an** apple.

examples.urdu: وہ سکول کا سب سے لمبا لڑکا ہے۔
examples.note: **The** is used with superlative adjectives.

examples.text: Give me **the** pen on the table.
examples.urdu: مجھے وہ قلم دیں جو میز پر ہے۔
examples.note: **The** refers to a specific pen.

commonMistakes.urdu: وہ ایک ایماندار آدمی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Use **an** because 'honest' starts with a vowel sound (h is silent).

commonMistakes.note: Use **a** for the first time you mention something non-specific.

commonMistakes.note: Use **a** because 'university' starts with a consonant sound (yoo).

types.name: Demonstratives
types.description: Demonstratives point to specific nouns and indicate their distance from the speaker.
types.urduExplanation: اشارہ کرنے والے الفاظ مخصوص اسموں کی طرف اشارہ کرتے ہیں اور بولنے والے سے ان کے فاصلے کو ظاہر کرتے ہیں۔
types.exampleWords: this, that, these, those
rules: 1: Use **this** for a singular noun that is near the speaker.
2: Use **that** for a singular noun that is far from the speaker.
3: Use **these** for plural nouns that are near the speaker.
4: Use **those** for plural nouns that are far from the speaker.
5: Demonstratives must agree in number with the noun they modify.
ruleExamples:
**This** book is mine.
**This** pen is blue. > Singular near: **this**.

**That** house is beautiful.
**That** star is bright. > Singular far: **that**.

**These** flowers are fresh.
**These** boys are my friends. > Plural near: **these**.

**Those** birds are flying south.
**Those** mountains are high. > Plural far: **those**.
❌ **This** books are new. ✅ **These** books are new. > Agreement rule.

examples.text: **This** book is mine.
examples.urdu: یہ کتاب میری ہے۔
examples.note: **This** refers to a singular object nearby.

examples.text: **That** house is beautiful.
examples.urdu: وہ گھر خوبصورت ہے۔

examples.note: **Those** refers to plural objects at a distance.

commonMistakes.urdu: مجھے وہ کتاب چاہیے۔
commonMistakes.note: Demonstratives directly modify the noun.

types.name: Possessives
types.description: Possessive determiners show who owns or possesses a noun.
types.urduExplanation: ملکیتی الفاظ یہ ظاہر کرتے ہیں کہ کسی اسم کا مالک کون ہے یا وہ کس کی ملکیت میں ہے۔
types.exampleWords: my, your, his, her, its, our, their
rules: 1: Use **my** for something belonging to me.
2: Use **your** for something belonging to you.
3: Use **his** for a male and **her** for a female possessor.
4: Use **its** for animals or non-living things.
5: Use **our** for something belonging to us and **their** for something belonging to them.
6: Do not confuse possessive determiners with possessive pronouns (e.g., my vs. mine).
ruleExamples:
This is **my** bag.
**My** father is a teacher. > Belonging to me: **my**.

Is this **your** pen?
**Your** house is big. > Belonging to you: **your**.

**His** name is Ali.
**Her** dress is pink. > Male/Female possession.

The dog wagged **its** tail.
The tree lost **its** leaves. > Animal/Thing: **its**.

**Our** team won.
**Their** parents are here. > We/They possession.
❌ This is **mine** bag. ✅ This is **my** bag. > Determiner vs. Pronoun.

examples.text: This is **my** bag.
examples.urdu: یہ میرا بیگ ہے۔
examples.note: **My** shows my possession.

examples.text: **His** name is Ali.
examples.urdu: اس کا نام علی ہے۔
examples.note: **His** refers to a male possessor.

examples.text: The dog wagged **its** tail.
